title: Regex basics - preg_match, delimiters, and character classes
answer: A regex pattern sits between delimiters, usually slashes. \d matches a digit, \w matches a word character, + means one or more, and ^ and $ anchor the start and end. preg_match returns 1 on a match, 0 on no match, and false on an invalid pattern.
pitfall: Forgetting ^ and $ lets a pattern match part of a string. A 10-digit check without anchors accepts a 20-digit number that contains 10 digits.

title: Regex replace and split - preg_replace, preg_split, and capture groups
answer: preg_replace swaps every match, with $1, $2 referring to capture groups. preg_split breaks a string on a pattern, which handles messy separators better than explode. preg_match_all collects every match into an array.
pitfall: Replacement strings treat $ and \ specially. A literal dollar sign in the replacement needs escaping, or it will be read as a group reference.

title: Regex validation - emails, phone numbers, and slugs
answer: Use a strict pattern for phone numbers and slugs, and prefer filter_var for email validation instead of a hand-written email regex, which is easy to get wrong. Keep patterns anchored and reject anything that does not match fully.
pitfall: A phone pattern that accepts any 10 digits also accepts numbers starting with 0 or 1, which are not valid Indian mobile numbers. Anchor the first digit to 6-9.
